item.title: The Crew
item.description:
The Crew

Recruiting for the bridge. Nothing is for sale here — I am looking for minds.

This blog is the flight log of a scout vessel that has been orbiting the NASDAQ Galaxy for over a year, describing its physics: capital flow instead of narratives, volume instead of opinions, options structure instead of forecasts. At the helm sits a human — the Architect — and beside him works Heniu: a local cognitive exoskeleton, a machine that watches the tape from open to close and feels no emotions at a margin call.

item.title: CVD — Cumulative Volume Delta, the Fuel of the System
item.description:
CVD — Cumulative Volume Delta

In the Antigravity cosmology: Fuel / Energy Flow. In classical language: the cumulative difference between aggressively bought and aggressively sold volume.

What CVD really is

Every market transaction has two sides, but only one of them is the aggressor: someone crossed the spread because they wanted in now, at market price. CVD sums those decisions: trades executed at the ask (aggressive buying) count as plus, at the bid (aggressive selling) as minus. The result is a running balance of wanting: who is paying for immediacy — demand or supply.

item.title: MOC — the Closing Imbalance, a.k.a. the MOC Anomaly
item.description:
MOC — Market-On-Close Imbalance

In the Antigravity cosmology: the MOC Anomaly / the MOC Hammer — a gravitational strike in the final minutes of the cycle. In classical language: the order imbalance into the close — the surplus of demand or supply the exchange must pair off by 4:00 PM New York time.

What MOC really is

A vast share of market capital — index funds, ETFs — settles by definition at the closing price. Their orders flow into a special closing auction, and a few minutes before the end of the session the exchange publishes the imbalance: how much more there is to buy than to sell (or the reverse). It is the only moment of the day when big capital must show its hand — the flow is declared, not inferred.

item.title: TICKQ — Nasdaq Market Breadth, a.k.a. Background Radiation
item.description:
TICKQ — Nasdaq Market Breadth

In the Antigravity cosmology: Background Radiation; its SMA200 average is the Mean Radiation. In classical language: a breadth indicator — the number of Nasdaq stocks ticking up at a given instant minus the number ticking down.

What TICKQ really is

An index price can lie through concentration: five Core singularities can drag NDX upward while hundreds of smaller bodies fall. TICKQ measures what the index price cannot show: whether the whole galaxy is breathing together. A reading of +600 means that at this second six hundred more stocks are ticking up than down — a broad market, a move carried by mass. A reading of −600 is panic across the entire population, regardless of what the giants are doing.
